newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany charges two guerrillas over bomb attacks.
newsitem.headline: Germany charges two guerrillas over bomb attacks.

text.p: Two suspected guerrillas from a shadowy group called the Anti-Imperialist Cell (AIZ) have been charged with attempted murder for a spate of bomb attacks on politicians, German prosecutors said on Tuesday.

The two men -- identified only as Bernhard F, 29 years old, and Michael S, 30 -- were charged with five counts of attempted murder and membership of a terrorist organisation, the Federal Prosecutor's Office said in a statement.

The AIZ depicts itself as a successor to the Red Army Faction (RAF), once known as the Baader-Meinhof Gang, which waged war on the German establishment with kidnappings and assassinations in the 1970s and 1980s.

The statement said the AIZ, which aimed to continue the "anti-imperialist fight" against state and society in Germany, had claimed responsibility for a series of bomb attacks in 1994 and 1995 on the homes of second-tier conservative politicians.
There were no casualties but the AIZ said it was prepared to put lives at risk.

The two men, who were arrested in February last year, were charged with planning and executing six bomb attacks including one on a Peruvian honorary consulate in Duesseldorf in December 1995, which slightly injured several people.

The prosecutor's statement said the two men had also produced and distributed letters claiming responsibility for the attacks in which the AIZ said it would use "potentially lethal acts to put pressure on elites".
The men were also suspected of planning an attack on the AIZ's next target -- Freimut Duve, member of parliament for the centre-left Social Democrat (SPD) opposition.
The statement said the suspects had acquired a large amount of gunpowder and had watched Duve's house in Hamburg. The suspects were detained during these preparations.
German media reports suggested Duve had been targeted because he had come out strongly in favour of letting German troops join multinational peacekeepers in Bosnia.
Germany's anti-extremist Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) said last year the AIZ's ethos of violence had made it a pariah even amongst other extreme left-wing groups.

The BfV said the circle of AIZ sympathisers and activists probably numbered about 30 to 50 people, and they took as their models groups as diverse as the RAF, Peru's Shining Path Maoist guerrillas, Algerian Islamists and Chechen rebels.
